module_title: Scaling Up Production and Team Building

lessons.title: Hiring and Training Apprentices
lessons.body:
When you start getting more orders than you can handle alone, it's time to hire apprentices. In many African countries, you can find young people eager to learn a trade through local vocational centres, church groups, or by word of mouth. Look for someone reliable, physically fit, and willing to learnânot necessarily with experience. A good apprentice shows up on time, listens, and isn't afraid to get their hands dirty. Start with one or two apprentices, and pay them a fair daily wage or a small monthly stipend. For example, in Nigeria, a ceramic apprentice might earn â¦3,000ââ¦5,000 per day, depending on the region. In Kenya, KSh 500â800 per day is common. Pay on time, every timeâthat builds trust.

Training should be hands-on and structured. Don't just tell them what to do; show them. Break tasks into simple steps: wedging clay, operating the pug mill, casting in moulds, operating the kiln, glazing, and packing. Use the 'I do, we do, you do' method. First, you demonstrate. Then you do it together. Then you watch them do it. Give immediate feedbackâpraise what's right, correct what's wrong gently. For example, when teaching how to prepare clay for throwing, show them how to wedge properly to remove air bubbles. Let them practice on 5 kg of clay, then check for even consistency. Repeat until they can do it without you.

Safety is non-negotiable. Before any apprentice touches a machine or kiln, teach them basic safety: wear a dust mask when mixing dry materials, use gloves when handling glazes, and never touch a hot kiln. Also, teach them to respect the toolsâa broken mould or a cracked kiln shelf costs money. Set clear rules: no phone use while operating machinery, no running in the workshop, and always clean up after yourself. Consider a buddy system where a more experienced worker mentors a new one.

As apprentices improve, give them more responsibility. Start them on simple tasks like wedging clay or sanding greenware, then move them to casting, glazing, and eventually kiln firing. After 3â6 months, you'll know who is serious. Reward good work with a small bonus or a title like 'senior apprentice'. This motivates them and reduces turnover. Remember, a well-trained apprentice can become your most valuable team memberâor even a future partner. Treat them with respect, and they'll help your business grow.

lessons.title: Setting Up an Efficient Workshop Layout
lessons.body:
A well-planned workshop saves time, reduces accidents, and increases production. The goal is to arrange your space so that materials flow smoothly from one stage to the next with minimal backtracking. Think of your production line: raw materials come in, clay is prepared, pieces are formed, dried, fired, glazed, fired again, and finally packed for sale. Each step should have its own zone, arranged in a logical sequence. For example, store dry clay and additives near the mixing area. The mixing area should be close to the forming area (wheels or casting tables). Greenware drying racks should be near the kiln, and the glazing area should be between the kiln and the packing area. This reduces the distance workers walk and the risk of dropping pieces.

Space is often limited in African workshops, so use vertical storage. Build shelves from floor to ceiling for moulds, tools, and finished goods. Use pallets or wooden crates for bulk raw materials like clay, feldspar, and silica. Keep walkways at least 1 metre wide for safe movement. If you have a kiln, place it in a corner with good ventilationâpreferably near an outside wall with a chimney or exhaust fan. Never store flammable materials like gas cylinders or solvents near the kiln. Also, ensure there is a clear emergency exit.

Work surfaces should be at a comfortable height for the workers. For standing tasks like wedging or glazing, a bench height of 90â95 cm works well. For seated tasks like throwing, the wheel head should be at about 75â80 cm. Provide stools or mats to reduce fatigue. Lighting is critical: use natural light where possible, and add LED bulbs (at least 500 lumens per square metre) over work areas. Shadows cause mistakes. If you work with lead glazes, install a washbasin with soap and water near the glazing areaâworkers must wash hands before eating or smoking.

Organise tools with shadow boards or labelled bins. A place for everything and everything in its place. This cuts down on time wasted searching for a rib, sponge, or calipers. Keep a small maintenance corner with spanners, oil, and spare parts for your pug mill, wheel, or kiln. Finally, plan for expansion: leave some empty space for a second kiln or an extra worktable. A good layout grows with your business. Review it every 6 months and adjust as needed. Ask your apprentices for feedbackâthey often see inefficiencies you miss.

lessons.title: Batch Production Systems
lessons.body:
Batch production means making many identical items in one go, rather than one at a time. This is the key to scaling up. Instead of throwing one bowl, you throw 20. Instead of glazing one tile, you glaze 100. Batch production saves time, reduces waste, and ensures consistency. For example, if you make 50 mugs in a batch, you can mix one large batch of clay, wedge it once, and throw all 50 in a day. Then you let them dry together, fire them together, and glaze them together. This is far more efficient than making one mug from start to finish before starting the next.

Start by planning your batch size based on your kiln capacity. If your kiln can fire 100 mugs per load, then make batches of 100. If you have a smaller kiln, say 30 pieces, then batch 30. Always make a few extra (5â10%) to account for breakages during drying, firing, and glazing. For example, if you need 100 good tiles, make 110. Keep a production log: date, product, batch number, quantity, and any notes. This helps you track costs and identify problems.

Organise your team into a production line. One person can wedge clay, another can throw, another can trim, another can glaze. This division of labour speeds things up. But be careful: each person must be trained to do their task well. If one person is slow, the whole line suffers. So cross-train everyone so they can rotate and cover for each other. For example, in a small workshop in Ghana, a team of four can produce 200 glazed tiles per day if they work in a batch system: one mixes clay, two press tiles, one glazes and fires. That's 1,000 tiles per weekâenough to supply local builders.

Standardise your products. Use moulds, jigs, and templates. For tiles, make a wooden frame that fits your press. For mugs, use a measuring stick to get the same height. Write down the exact measurements, clay weight, glaze recipe, and firing schedule. This is your standard operating procedure (SOP). Once you have an SOP, anyone can make the same product. That's how you grow. Also, keep raw materials organised by batch: pre-weighed bags of clay, pre-measured glaze ingredients. This reduces errors and speeds up production. Finally, schedule your batches so that drying and firing times overlap. While one batch is in the kiln, you can be forming the next batch. This keeps the workshop productive every day.

lessons.title: Quality Assurance in Larger Scale
lessons.body:
When you were making one pot at a time, you could check every piece by eye. But with batch production, you need a system to ensure quality. Quality assurance (QA) means checking at every stage, not just at the end. If you wait until after firing to find defects, you've wasted clay, labour, and kiln fuel. So build checks into your process. For example, after mixing clay, test a small sample for plasticity and shrinkage. After forming, check for cracks, warping, or uneven thickness. After drying, check for hairline cracks. After bisque firing, check for dunts (cracks from firing). After glazing, check for missed spots or drips. After glaze firing, check for colour consistency and glaze fit.

Use simple tools: a ruler, calipers, a scale, and a moisture meter. For tiles, check dimensions with a square and measure thickness at several points. For mugs, check handle strength by hanging a 500g weight for 10 seconds. For glazes, keep a fired test tile from each batch to compare colour. If you use a kiln, use pyrometric cones or a digital controller to ensure consistent temperature. Record every batch's results in a log. If you see a pattern of defects, trace it back to the cause. For example, if 10% of tiles are warping, maybe the clay is too wet or the drying is too fast. Adjust and retest.

Train your workers to be their own quality inspectors. Give them the authority to stop production if they see a problem. For example, if a moulder notices that the clay is too stiff, they should tell the mixer immediately. Reward workers who catch defects early. Also, set a standard for acceptable quality: what percentage of defects is okay? In small-scale production, aim for less than 5% rejects. If you have more than 10%, you're losing money. Keep a reject bin and analyse the rejects weekly. Are they all from one mould? One worker? One batch of clay? Fix the root cause.

Finally, get feedback from your customers. Ask them if the tiles are the right size, if the colours match, if the products are durable. Use that feedback to improve. In larger scale, consistency is your reputation. A builder who buys 500 tiles expects them all to be the same. If 10 are a different shade, he may reject the whole batch. So invest in QA. It saves money in the long run and builds trust. Remember, quality is not an accident; it's a habit.

lessons.title: Purchasing Raw Materials in Bulk
lessons.body:
Buying raw materials in bulk can save you 20â40% on costs, but it requires planning and cash. Start by calculating your monthly usage. For example, if you make 1,000 tiles per month, and each tile uses 1.5 kg of clay, you need 1,500 kg (1.5 tonnes) of clay per month. Add 10% for waste, so 1.65 tonnes. If you buy in 25 kg bags, that's 66 bags. Buying 66 bags at once often gets you a discount from the supplier. In many African countries, you can find clay suppliers near brick factories or ceramic raw material dealers. For example, in South Africa, you can buy from suppliers like Ceramic Supplies or local brick yards. In Nigeria, check markets like Oshodi or local mining areas.

Before you buy, test the material. Never buy a tonne of clay without testing a small sample. Make a few test tiles, fire them, and check for shrinkage, colour, and defects. Ask the supplier for a certificate of analysis if available. For glazes, buy chemicals like frit, silica, feldspar, and colourants in 25 kg drums or bags. Store them in a dry, ventilated area away from moisture. Use airtight containers for hygroscopic materials like soda ash or borax. Label everything clearly: name, date, and safety warnings.

Negotiate with suppliers. Ask for a discount for bulk and for repeat business. Sometimes you can get better prices if you pay cash on delivery. Consider forming a buying cooperative with other ceramic businesses in your area. Together, you can order a full truckload and split the cost. This is common in Kenya and Ghana. Also, look for local alternatives: rice husk ash can be used as a source of silica; local clay can be blended with imported kaolin. This reduces costs and supports local economy.

Storage is key. Build a dry store with pallets to keep bags off the floor. Moisture ruins clay and chemicals. Use a first-in, first-out (FIFO) system: always use the oldest stock first. Keep an inventory book or a simple spreadsheet. Record date of purchase, quantity, and supplier. Reorder when stock reaches a reorder level (e.g., two weeks' worth of production). Don't tie up all your cash in stockâbalance bulk savings with cash flow. Start with a 2-month supply, then increase as you grow. Finally, transport: if you buy in bulk, arrange your own transport or negotiate delivery. A pick-up truck can carry 1 tonne. Always check the weight and quality on delivery before you pay.

lessons.title: Health and Safety for Workers
lessons.body:
Ceramics can be hazardous if you don't take precautions. Dust from clay and glaze materials can cause silicosis, a serious lung disease. Kilns produce carbon monoxide and can cause burns. Glazes may contain lead or other toxic metals. So you must protect yourself and your workers. First, control dust. Mix dry materials in a well-ventilated area, ideally outdoors or with a fan blowing away from you. Wear a NIOSH-approved N95 dust mask when mixing or sanding. Never sweep dry dustâuse a wet mop or a vacuum with a HEPA filter. Keep surfaces damp when cleaning. For example, in a workshop in Tanzania, workers wet down the floor before sweeping to keep dust down.

Second, handle chemicals safely. Wear gloves and goggles when mixing glazes. Never eat, drink, or smoke in the glazing area. Wash hands thoroughly after handling glaze materials, especially before eating. If you use lead glazes, switch to lead-free frit if possible. Lead is banned in many countries for food-contact ceramics. If you must use lead, use a fume hood and a respirator. Store chemicals in labelled containers, away from food and children. Keep a first-aid kit with burn cream, bandages, and eye wash.

Third, kiln safety. Kilns are hotâup to 1300Â°C. Never open a kiln until it has cooled below 100Â°C. Use heat-resistant gloves and a face shield when unloading. Ensure the kiln area has good ventilation to avoid carbon monoxide buildup. Install a carbon monoxide detector if you use a gas kiln. Keep a fire extinguisher (CO2 or dry powder) near the kiln. Never leave a firing kiln unattended. Train everyone on emergency shutdown procedures. Also, check electrical connections regularlyâloose wires can cause fires.

Fourth, ergonomics and general safety. Pottery involves repetitive movements and heavy lifting. Teach workers to lift with their legs, not their backs. Provide stools or anti-fatigue mats. Rotate tasks to avoid repetitive strain. Keep walkways clear. Store heavy items on lower shelves. Use trolleys for moving heavy clay bags. Have a strict no-running rule. Finally, create a safety culture. Hold a 5-minute safety talk every Monday. Ask workers to report hazards. Reward safe behaviour. Post safety rules in local language with pictures. Keep a accident log and review it monthly. A safe workshop is a productive workshop. Your workers' health is your business's health.

quiz.q: What is a good way to find apprentices for your ceramic workshop?
options: A) Post on international job websites
B) Ask local vocational centres and church groups
D) Wait for people to walk in off the street
quiz.explanation: Local vocational centres and community groups are effective for finding eager learners in African contexts.

quiz.q: When training an apprentice, which method is recommended?
options: A) Tell them once and expect perfection
B) Use the 'I do, we do, you do' method
C) Let them learn by trial and error alone
D) Give them a manual to read
quiz.explanation: The 'I do, we do, you do' method ensures hands-on learning with immediate feedback.

quiz.q: What should you teach an apprentice before they operate a kiln?
options: A) How to calculate firing costs
B) Basic safety rules and kiln operation
C) How to design new products
D) How to market products online
quiz.explanation: Safety is non-negotiable; apprentices must learn safety rules before using any equipment.

quiz.q: How often should you pay apprentices to build trust?
options: A) Whenever you feel like it
C) Only after they finish training
quiz.explanation: Paying on time builds trust and motivation.

quiz.q: What is a good way to motivate apprentices?
options: A) Give them a small bonus for good work
D) Give them all the hardest tasks
quiz.explanation: Rewarding good work with bonuses or titles reduces turnover.

quiz.q: In an efficient workshop layout, what should be placed near the kiln?
options: B) Greenware drying racks and glazing area
quiz.explanation: Placing drying racks and glazing near the kiln reduces movement and breakage.

quiz.q: Why is vertical storage recommended in small workshops?
quiz.explanation: Vertical storage maximizes limited floor space.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum width for walkways in a workshop?
quiz.explanation: A 1-metre walkway allows safe movement of people and materials.

quiz.q: Where should a kiln be placed for safety?
options: A) In the middle of the workshop
B) Near an outside wall with good ventilation
quiz.explanation: Good ventilation prevents carbon monoxide buildup.

quiz.q: What is a shadow board used for?
options: B) To organise tools with outlines
quiz.explanation: Shadow boards keep tools organised and easily accessible.

quiz.q: What is batch production?
options: A) Making one item at a time
B) Making many identical items in one go
C) Making different items each day
D) Only making items to order
quiz.explanation: Batch production means producing many identical items together for efficiency.

quiz.q: Why should you make extra pieces in a batch?
options: B) To account for breakages and defects
C) To use up all clay
quiz.explanation: Making 5â10% extra ensures you meet the required number of good pieces.

quiz.q: What is an SOP in ceramics production?
quiz.explanation: SOP stands for Standard Operating Procedure, which ensures consistency.

quiz.q: How can you speed up production in a batch system?
options: A) Have one person do all tasks
B) Use a production line with division of labour
C) Work slower to avoid mistakes
D) Only work when orders come
quiz.explanation: Division of labour speeds up production by specialising tasks.

quiz.q: What should you do while one batch is firing in the kiln?
options: B) Start forming the next batch
quiz.explanation: Overlapping tasks keeps the workshop productive.

quiz.q: What is quality assurance?
options: A) Checking only the final product
B) Checking at every stage of production
quiz.explanation: Quality assurance means checking throughout the process, not just at the end.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for checking tile dimensions?
quiz.explanation: A ruler and square ensure tiles meet size specifications.

quiz.q: What is an acceptable reject rate for small-scale production?
quiz.explanation: Aim for less than 5% rejects to remain profitable.

quiz.q: Why is customer feedback important for quality?
options: A) It helps improve products and consistency
quiz.explanation: Customer feedback identifies areas for improvement and builds reputation.

quiz.q: What should you do with rejected pieces?
options: A) Sell them as first quality
B) Analyse them to find the root cause
quiz.explanation: Analysing rejects helps fix production problems.

quiz.q: How much can you save by buying raw materials in bulk?
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying typically saves 20â40% on material costs.

quiz.q: What should you do before buying a large quantity of clay?
quiz.explanation: Always test a sample to ensure quality before committing to bulk purchase.

quiz.q: Why is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) system important for raw materials?
options: A) It ensures older stock is used first
quiz.explanation: FIFO prevents materials from expiring or deteriorating.

quiz.q: What is a buying cooperative?
options: A) A group of businesses buying together for discounts
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives pool orders to get bulk discounts.

quiz.q: How should you store hygroscopic chemicals?
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers prevent moisture absorption.

quiz.q: What is a health hazard in ceramics from dry clay dust?
quiz.explanation: Silicosis is a lung disease caused by inhaling silica dust.

quiz.q: What should you wear when mixing dry glaze materials?
quiz.explanation: A dust mask prevents inhalation of toxic particles.

quiz.q: Why is lead glaze dangerous?
options: A) It is toxic and banned for food-contact ceramics
C) It is hard to mix
quiz.explanation: Lead can leach into food and cause poisoning.

quiz.q: When is it safe to open a kiln?
options: B) When it has cooled below 100Â°C
D) When it stops making noise
quiz.explanation: Opening a hot kiln can cause severe burns and thermal shock to ware.

quiz.q: What should you have near the kiln for safety?
quiz.explanation: A fire extinguisher is essential for kiln emergencies.
